items.stem: What is the correct order of taxa from highest to lowest?
options: domain, phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, genus, species
kingdom, domain, class, phylum, order, family, genus, species
species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom, domain
domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
items.answer: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
items.markingKey: D. Mnemonic: Do Keep Ponds Clean Or Frogs Get Sick.

items.stem: Which statement about ecological niches: obligate and facultative modes of nutrition is not correct?
options: All bacteria need oxygen to survive.
Obligate anaerobe is an organism that can only survive in the absence of oxygen, for which oxygen is toxic.
Ecological niche is the role of a species in an ecosystem, including its habitat, its use of resources and all its interactions with other species and abiotic factors.
Facultative anaerobe is an organism that respires aerobically when oxygen is present but can switch to anaerobic respiration when it is absent.
items.answer: All bacteria need oxygen to survive.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “All bacteria need oxygen to survive.” – Many bacteria are facultative or obligate anaerobes; some are killed by oxygen.

items.stem: Which atom in a water molecule carries a partial negative charge?
options: hydrogen
both hydrogen atoms equally
neither, because water is non-polar
oxygen
items.answer: oxygen
items.markingKey: D. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls the shared electrons towards itself and becomes δ−.

items.stem: The human insulin gene was inserted into bacteria, which produced functional human insulin. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (the production of human insulin by genetically modified Escherichia coli)?
options: The structural differences between RNA and DNA
The universality of the genetic code and base sequence as information
How evidence was used to build the model of DNA structure
The use of radioactive labelling to test a hypothesis
items.answer: The universality of the genetic code and base sequence as information
items.markingKey: B. Bacteria read the same codons as human cells, so the human base sequence is translated into the same amino acid sequence.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about stem cells, differentiation and gene expression is false?
options: Pluripotent is describes a stem cell that can differentiate into any cell type of the body, but not the placenta (e.g. embryonic stem cells).
Totipotent cells (zygote) can form all cell types including the placenta.
Adult stem cells can become any cell type.
Multipotent is describes a stem cell able to differentiate into a limited range of related cell types (e.g. bone marrow stem cells).
items.answer: Adult stem cells can become any cell type.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “Adult stem cells can become any cell type.” – Most adult stem cells are multipotent, forming only related cell types.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "polymer"?
options: A fatty acid with no carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain
A lipid with a structure of four fused carbon rings, such as cholesterol, oestradiol and testosterone
A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units joined by covalent bonds
A protein with carbohydrate chains attached, often found in the plasma membrane with the carbohydrate facing outwards
items.answer: A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units joined by covalent bonds
items.markingKey: C. "polymer" is a large molecule made of many repeating monomer units joined by covalent bonds.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about gas exchange in leaves: stomata and transpiration is false?
options: Spongy mesophyll is loosely packed leaf cells with large air spaces that allow diffusion of gases to and from photosynthesising cells.
Transpiration is largely an unavoidable consequence of stomata being open for CO₂ uptake.
Palisade mesophyll is tightly packed columnar cells with many chloroplasts, specialised for photosynthesis.
Stomata are open at night to take in CO₂.
items.answer: Stomata are open at night to take in CO₂.
items.markingKey: D. The incorrect statement is “Stomata are open at night to take in CO₂.” – In most plants stomata close in darkness because CO₂ is not needed for photosynthesis; CAM plants are an exception.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "amino acid"?
options: Regular folding of the polypeptide backbone into α-helices or β-pleated sheets, stabilised by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups
The variable side chain of an amino acid, which determines its properties (e.g. polar, non-polar, charged)
The three-dimensional folding of a whole polypeptide, stabilised by interactions between R groups
The monomer of proteins, with a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R group
items.answer: The monomer of proteins, with a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R group
items.markingKey: D. "amino acid" is the monomer of proteins, with a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R group.

items.stem: The amoeba contains photosynthetic “chromatophores” derived from a cyanobacterium about 100 million years ago. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (Paulinella chromatophora, an amoeba with a recently acquired cyanobacterial endosymbiont)?
options: The lytic cycle
How conditions on early Earth may have produced organic molecules
Endosymbiosis as an ongoing process
Prokaryotic cell structure
items.answer: Endosymbiosis as an ongoing process
items.markingKey: C. It shows a stage in which an engulfed prokaryote is becoming an organelle, as proposed for chloroplasts.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about biodiversity at ecosystem, species and genetic levels is false?
options: Biodiversity only refers to the number of species.
Biodiversity is the variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations, including ecosystem, species and genetic diversity.
Species evenness is how similar the abundances of the different species in an area are.
Simpson’s reciprocal index is a measure of species diversity, D = N(N − 1)/Σn(n − 1), that takes account of both richness and evenness.
items.answer: Biodiversity only refers to the number of species.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “Biodiversity only refers to the number of species.” – Biodiversity includes ecosystem, species and genetic diversity.

items.stem: In the binomial name of the lion, Panthera leo, what does each word represent?
options: Panthera is the family and leo is the genus.
Both words together name the genus.
Panthera is the species and leo is the genus.
Panthera is the genus and leo is the specific name.
items.answer: Panthera is the genus and leo is the specific name.
items.markingKey: D. Genus first (capitalised), specific name second (lower case), both italicised or underlined when handwritten.

items.stem: Which statement about in situ and ex situ conservation; EDGE of Existence is not correct?
options: Zoos alone can save endangered species from extinction.
In situ conservation protects species within their natural habitats (e.g. reserves).
EDGE species is a species that is both Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered, prioritised for conservation by the EDGE of Existence programme.
Seed bank is a facility that stores seeds under cold, dry conditions to conserve plant genetic diversity, e.g. the Svalbard Global Seed Vault.
items.answer: Zoos alone can save endangered species from extinction.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “Zoos alone can save endangered species from extinction.” – Zoos can maintain populations, but unless habitats are protected and threats removed, species cannot be returned to the wild; in situ conservation is essential.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The smaller type of ribosome found in prokaryotes (and mitochondria and chloroplasts)"?
options: protocell
freeze-fracture electron microscopy
70S ribosome
cryogenic electron microscopy
items.answer: 70S ribosome
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of 70S ribosome.

items.stem: Splitting frozen membranes along the middle revealed bumps (proteins) on the fracture faces. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (freeze-fracture electron micrographs of membranes)?
options: Adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity
Exocytosis
Osmosis and isotonic solutions
The falsification of the Davson–Danielli model
items.answer: The falsification of the Davson–Danielli model
items.markingKey: D. Proteins were seen within the bilayer, not just on its surfaces, so the sandwich model had to be rejected.

items.stem: Why does the tertiary structure of a globular protein cause hydrophobic R groups to be in the interior?
options: Hydrophilic R groups are repelled by water.
Disulfide bonds pull all hydrophobic groups inward.
Hydrophobic R groups avoid water and cluster together in the centre, while hydrophilic groups face the aqueous surroundings.
Hydrophobic R groups form peptide bonds in the centre.
items.answer: Hydrophobic R groups avoid water and cluster together in the centre, while hydrophilic groups face the aqueous surroundings.
items.markingKey: C. Hydrophobic interactions drive folding.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "divergent evolution"?
options: The cumulative change in the heritable characteristics of a population over time
The accumulation of differences between related populations, often leading to new species with different adaptations
A limb with five digits and a common bone pattern (humerus, radius and ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) found in tetrapods
Reproductive isolation caused by populations breeding at different times of day or year
items.answer: The accumulation of differences between related populations, often leading to new species with different adaptations
items.markingKey: B. "divergent evolution" is the accumulation of differences between related populations, often leading to new species with different adaptations.

items.stem: Which statement about simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis is not correct?
options: Aquaporin is a channel protein in the membrane that allows rapid passage of water molecules.
In osmosis, water moves from low water concentration to high water concentration.
Osmosis is the net passive movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration.
Both are passive and move substances down a concentration gradient.
items.answer: In osmosis, water moves from low water concentration to high water concentration.
items.markingKey: B. The incorrect statement is “In osmosis, water moves from low water concentration to high water concentration.” – Water moves from a region of lower solute concentration (higher water potential) to higher solute concentration (lower water potential).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "monosaccharide"?
options: A reaction in which two molecules are joined by a covalent bond with the release of a molecule of water
A small molecule that can be joined to others of the same type to form a polymer
The ability of cells to identify other cells, e.g. as self or non-self, using molecules such as glycoproteins on the cell surface
A single sugar unit such as glucose, fructose or galactose, the monomer of carbohydrates
items.answer: A single sugar unit such as glucose, fructose or galactose, the monomer of carbohydrates
items.markingKey: D. "monosaccharide" is a single sugar unit such as glucose, fructose or galactose, the monomer of carbohydrates.

items.stem: Pond water samples are tested for newt DNA as an accepted alternative to night-time torch and netting surveys before development. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (eDNA monitoring of great crested newts (Triturus cristatus) in ponds in England)?
options: The use of eDNA in identifying species
How cladistics leads to reclassification
The three-domain system of classification
Natural classification using molecular evidence
items.answer: The use of eDNA in identifying species
items.markingKey: A. Presence of the protected species is detected quickly and non-invasively from water samples.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about origins of cells: conditions on early Earth, Miller-Urey and endosymbiosis is false?
options: The first cells probably used DNA and proteins just like modern cells.
Abiogenesis is the origin of life from non-living matter through natural chemical processes.
Protocell is a self-organised, membrane-bound compartment of organic molecules proposed as a precursor of living cells.
It produced only simple organic molecules such as amino acids, not polymers or cells.
items.answer: The first cells probably used DNA and proteins just like modern cells.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “The first cells probably used DNA and proteins just like modern cells.” – The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA served as both genetic material and catalyst before DNA and proteins evolved.

items.stem: Which blood group is called the “universal donor” for red blood cells in the ABO system?
options: A
AB
B
O
items.answer: O
items.markingKey: D. O cells carry neither A nor B antigen.

items.stem: Which statement about differences between DNA and RNA is not correct?
options: DNA contains deoxyribose, thymine and is usually double-stranded.
Deoxyribose is the pentose sugar in DNA nucleotides, which lacks an oxygen (has H instead of OH) on carbon 2′.
RNA contains thymine and deoxyribose, just like DNA.
Ribose has a hydroxyl group on carbon 2′.
items.answer: RNA contains thymine and deoxyribose, just like DNA.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “RNA contains thymine and deoxyribose, just like DNA.” – RNA contains uracil instead of thymine and ribose instead of deoxyribose.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The monomer of a nucleic acid, made of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base"?
options: pyrimidine
ribose
nucleotide
complementary base pairing
items.answer: nucleotide
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of nucleotide.

items.stem: A radioactive tracer of ¹⁴CO₂ was given to a leaf. Labelled sucrose was detected 0.6 m away after 40 minutes. What was the rate of translocation?
options: 0.9 m h⁻¹
1.5 m h⁻¹
24 m h⁻¹
items.answer: 0.9 m h⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. 0.6 m in 40 min = 0.9 m per hour.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about evidence for evolution: base sequences, selective breeding and homologous structures is false?
options: Homologous structures always have the same function.
Evolution is the cumulative change in the heritable characteristics of a population over time.
Pentadactyl limb is a limb with five digits and a common bone pattern (humerus, radius and ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) found in tetrapods.
Selective breeding is artificial selection in which humans choose individuals with desired traits to breed, changing the characteristics of domesticated species over generations.
items.answer: Homologous structures always have the same function.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “Homologous structures always have the same function.” – Homologous structures share structure and origin, but often have different functions, e.g. bat wing and human arm.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "surfactant"?
options: A phospholipid–protein secretion from type II pneumocytes that reduces surface tension in alveoli and prevents their collapse
Pairs of specialised epidermal cells that change shape to open and close a stoma
Pairs of muscles that produce opposite movements at a joint, such as biceps and triceps
The thin filament protein with binding sites for myosin heads
items.answer: A phospholipid–protein secretion from type II pneumocytes that reduces surface tension in alveoli and prevents their collapse
items.markingKey: A. "surfactant" is a phospholipid–protein secretion from type II pneumocytes that reduces surface tension in alveoli and prevents their collapse.

items.stem: Which statement about range of tolerance, transects and biomes is not correct?
options: Correlation does not prove causation.
Zonation is the gradual change in distribution of species across a habitat in response to an environmental gradient, such as on a rocky shore.
Quadrat is a square frame of known area used to sample organisms in a habitat.
The optimum range of tolerance is always at the edge of a species’ distribution.
items.answer: The optimum range of tolerance is always at the edge of a species’ distribution.
items.markingKey: D. The incorrect statement is “The optimum range of tolerance is always at the edge of a species’ distribution.” – The optimum is usually in the middle of the range; populations at the edges are under physiological stress.

items.stem: Which type of joint is the human elbow?
options: a fixed joint
a ball-and-socket joint
a synovial hinge joint
a cartilaginous joint
items.answer: a synovial hinge joint
items.markingKey: C. Allows flexion and extension.

items.stem: Closely related species carry different multiples of a basic chromosome set (for example P. hydropiper 2n = 20 and P. maculosa 2n = 44), reflecting polyploidy. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (the knotweed genus Persicaria)?
options: Convergent evolution
Analogous structures
Speciation by polyploidy
Allopatric speciation
items.answer: Speciation by polyploidy
items.markingKey: C. Doubling of chromosome sets created instant reproductive isolation and new species within the genus.

items.stem: Which statement about causes of the current biodiversity crisis and mass extinctions is not correct?
options: Extinctions only happened in the distant past, before humans.
Background extinction is the continuous low rate of species loss.
Anthropogenic is caused by human activity.
Monocultures such as oil palm support far fewer species than natural forest.
items.answer: Extinctions only happened in the distant past, before humans.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “Extinctions only happened in the distant past, before humans.” – Many species have gone extinct due to humans, e.g. the moa, dodo and passenger pigeon, and current rates are far above background levels.

items.stem: Which type of evidence is now most commonly used to construct cladograms?
options: habitat
colour
size of organisms
base sequences of DNA or amino acid sequences
items.answer: base sequences of DNA or amino acid sequences
items.markingKey: D. Sequence data provide many characters and are less prone to convergence.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about viruses: structure, lytic and lysogenic cycles is false?
options: A virus in the lysogenic cycle is inactive and harmless permanently.
Prophage is the DNA of a bacteriophage integrated into the bacterial chromosome during the lysogenic cycle.
Lysogenic cycle is a viral cycle in which viral DNA is integrated into the host chromosome as a prophage and copied with it, without immediate production of virions.
Envelope is a membrane derived from the host cell surrounding the capsid of some viruses, such as influenza and HIV.
items.answer: A virus in the lysogenic cycle is inactive and harmless permanently.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “A virus in the lysogenic cycle is inactive and harmless permanently.” – A prophage can be induced to enter the lytic cycle, e.g. by UV or stress, killing the host and releasing virions.

items.stem: Why do large bodies of water such as oceans have relatively stable temperatures?
options: Water has a low density.
Water does not conduct heat.
Water has a high specific heat capacity, so large energy changes produce small temperature changes.
Water reflects all sunlight.
items.answer: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so large energy changes produce small temperature changes.
items.markingKey: C. Many hydrogen bonds must be broken to raise the temperature.

items.stem: Their membranes contain a high proportion of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (Antarctic icefish living at −1.9 °C)?
options: Facilitated diffusion of water
Osmosis and isotonic solutions
Exocytosis
Adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity
items.answer: Adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity
items.markingKey: D. Kinked unsaturated chains prevent membranes becoming rigid at freezing temperatures.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about denaturation and the effect of pH and temperature is false?
options: Enzymes are killed by high temperatures.
Denaturation is a change in the three-dimensional structure of a protein, caused by breaking of the bonds that maintain it, so that it loses its biological activity.
Irreversible denaturation is denaturation after which the protein cannot return to its original shape, e.g. when egg albumin is cooked.
In reversible denaturation the protein refolds to its active shape when conditions return to normal (e.g. mild pH change).
items.answer: Enzymes are killed by high temperatures.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “Enzymes are killed by high temperatures.” – Enzymes are molecules, not living organisms; they are denatured, not killed.

items.stem: What is the realised niche of a species?
options: the part of its fundamental niche it actually occupies when competitors are present
its geographical range
its habitat only
the niche it would occupy without competitors
items.answer: the part of its fundamental niche it actually occupies when competitors are present
items.markingKey: A. Competition restricts the niche.

items.stem: Why do the semilunar valves open during ventricular systole?
options: Pressure in the ventricle rises above pressure in the artery.
The SA node opens them.
Muscles pull them open.
Pressure in the atria rises.
items.answer: Pressure in the ventricle rises above pressure in the artery.
items.markingKey: A. Valves respond to pressure differences.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "microvilli"?
options: Describes a stem cell that can differentiate into any cell type of the body, but not the placenta (e.g. embryonic stem cells)
The fluid surrounding the thylakoids in a chloroplast, containing enzymes of the Calvin cycle
Describes a stem cell able to differentiate into a limited range of related cell types (e.g. bone marrow stem cells)
Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane that increase surface area for absorption
items.answer: Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane that increase surface area for absorption
items.markingKey: D. "microvilli" is finger-like projections of the plasma membrane that increase surface area for absorption.

items.stem: Chloroplasts in shade leaves have larger grana with more thylakoids. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (shade leaves compared with sun leaves)?
options: The therapeutic use of stem cells
The structure–function relationship of chloroplasts
The secretory pathway and compartmentalisation
Gene expression in differentiation
items.answer: The structure–function relationship of chloroplasts
items.markingKey: B. More thylakoid membrane holds more light-harvesting pigment, capturing more of the limited light.

items.stem: Which statement about active transport, pump proteins and bulk transport (endocytosis and exocytosis) is not correct?
options: Active transport is the movement of particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP and specific pump proteins.
Pump protein is a membrane protein that uses energy (usually from ATP hydrolysis) to move specific particles against their concentration gradient.
Endocytosis and exocytosis require ATP to reshape the membrane and move vesicles, though they depend on membrane fluidity.
Active transport moves substances from high to low concentration.
items.answer: Active transport moves substances from high to low concentration.
items.markingKey: D. The incorrect statement is “Active transport moves substances from high to low concentration.” – Active transport moves substances from low to high concentration, against the gradient, using energy.

items.stem:
On Daphne Major in the Galápagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the beak depth of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis). A severe drought in 1977 reduced the supply of small, soft seeds; mainly large, hard seeds remained.

Year | Population | Mean beak depth / mm
1976 | 1398 | 9.17
1977 | 178 | 9.77
1978 | — | 9.67

The standard deviation of beak depth in 1976 was 1.05 mm.

(a) Calculate the percentage of the 1976 population that survived to 1977. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in mean beak depth from 1976 to 1977. [2]
(c) Explain why the offspring produced in 1978 also had deeper beaks than the 1976 population. [2]
(d) The change in mean beak depth was about 0.6 standard deviations. Comment on the size of this change. [1]
(e) Suggest why this study is described as evolution being observed in action. [1]
(f) State the type of selection shown by these data. [1]
items.answer: (a) 12.7 % (b) +6.5 % (c) Beak depth is heritable; survivors passed alleles for deeper beaks to their offspring, so allele frequencies changed – evolution. (d) Large for one generation; shows strong directional selection. (e) The change in a heritable characteristic of the population was measured over a single generation, rather than inferred from fossils. (f) directional selection
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 178/1398 × 100 (M1) = 12.7 % (A1). (b) [2] (9.77 − 9.17)/9.17 × 100 (M1) = +6.5 % (A1). (c) [2] Heritability (A1); allele frequency change between generations (A1). (d) [1] Recognises a substantial shift relative to natural variation (A1). (e) [1] Measured directly across generations / short time scale (A1). (f) [1] Directional (A1).

items.stem:
The table shows the number of carbon atoms, the number of cis C=C double bonds and the melting point of some fatty acids.

Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
palmitic acid | 16 | 0 | 62.9
stearic acid | 18 | 0 | 69.3
arachidic acid | 20 | 0 | 75.5
oleic acid | 18 | 1 | 13.4
linoleic acid | 18 | 2 | -5.0
α-linolenic acid | 18 | 3 | -11.0

(a) State the melting point of oleic acid. [1]
(b) Describe the effect of chain length on the melting point of saturated fatty acids. [2]
(c) Calculate the difference in melting point between stearic acid and oleic acid. [1]
(d) Calculate the percentage decrease in melting point from stearic to oleic acid. [2]
(e) Predict, with a reason, whether a fat rich in linoleic acid would be solid or liquid at 20 °C. [1]
(f) Suggest why fish living in cold water have more polyunsaturated fatty acids in their membranes. [2]
items.answer: (a) 13.4 °C (b) Melting point increases with chain length, by about 6.3 °C per two extra carbons. (c) 55.9 °C (d) 81 % (e) Liquid – its melting point (−5 °C) is below 20 °C. (f) Polyunsaturated fatty acids have low melting points, keeping membranes fluid at low temperatures so membrane proteins can function.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 13.4 °C (A1). (b) [2] Positive relationship (A1); quantified using data (A1). (c) [1] 69.3 − 13.4 = 55.9 °C (A1). (d) [2] (69.3 − 13.4)/69.3 × 100 (M1) = 81 % (A1). (e) [1] Liquid with data-based reason (A1). (f) [2] Low melting point / maintain fluidity (A1); link to membrane function (A1).

items.stem:
Hana supplied 10000 J of energy from an electric immersion heater to 150 g samples of water and of seawater, each in an insulated beaker, and recorded the temperature rise.

Liquid | Mass / g | Energy supplied / J | Temperature rise / °C
water | 150 | 10000 | 15.5
seawater | 150 | 10000 | 17.0

(a) State which liquid showed the greater temperature rise. [1]
(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of each liquid in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, using c = Q/(m ΔT). [2]
(c) Calculate how many percent greater the specific heat capacity of water is than that of seawater. [2]
(d) Explain why water has a high specific heat capacity. [2]
(e) Suggest one reason why the value obtained for water may differ from the accepted value of 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. [1]
(f) Suggest one improvement to the method. [1]
items.answer: (a) seawater (b) water 4.30; seawater 3.92 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (c) 10 % (d) Much of the energy supplied is used to break the many hydrogen bonds between water molecules rather than increasing their kinetic energy. (e) Heat lost to the surroundings/beaker; thermometer reading error; uneven mixing. (f) Stir the liquid; use a lid; repeat and calculate a mean; use a digital thermometer.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] seawater (A1). (b) [2] Water: 10000/(150 × 15.5) = 4.30 (A1); seawater: 10000/(150 × 17.0) = 3.92 (A1). (c) [2] (4.30 − 3.92)/3.92 × 100 (M1) = 10 % (A1). (d) [2] Hydrogen bonds between molecules (A1); energy used to break them before temperature rises (A1). (e) [1] Any valid source of error linked to the direction of the difference (A1). (f) [1] Any one valid improvement (A1).

items.stem:
Samples of lactate dehydrogenase from rabbit muscle (enzyme X) and the same enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium (enzyme Y) were held at different temperatures for 10 minutes, cooled to 25 °C and their remaining activity measured as a percentage of the untreated activity.

Temperature / °C | Enzyme X activity remaining / % | Enzyme Y activity remaining / %
30 | 100 | 100
40 | 97 | 100
50 | 69 | 100
60 | 11 | 100
70 | 1 | 99
80 | 0 | 82
90 | 0 | 21

(a) State the activity of enzyme X remaining after treatment at 60 °C. [1]
(b) Estimate the temperature at which each enzyme has lost half of its activity. [2]
(c) Compare the effect of temperature on enzymes X and Y. [2]
(d) Suggest how the structure of enzyme Y differs to make it more heat stable. [1]
(e) Suggest one industrial use of enzyme Y and justify it. [2]
items.answer: (a) 11 % (b) X ≈ 53 °C; Y ≈ 85 °C (c) Both retain full activity at low temperatures and lose activity as temperature rises; Y tolerates much higher temperatures before losing activity. (d) More disulfide bonds, ionic bonds (salt bridges) and hydrophobic interactions; more compact core. (e) PCR or biological washing powders/industrial processes at high temperature – remains active and reactions are faster at high temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 11 % (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation (M1); X 53 °C and Y 85 °C, accept ±2 °C (A1). (c) [2] Similarity (A1); difference with data (A1). (d) [1] Any valid structural difference (A1). (e) [2] Use (A1) with justification (R1).

items.stem:
In the Hershey–Chase experiment, E. coli infected with radioactively labelled T2 phage were agitated in a blender for different times. The percentage of each isotope released into the supernatant and the percentage of bacteria still infected were measured.

Blending time / min | ³⁵S released / % | ³²P released / %
0 | 0 | 0
1 | 46 | 18
2 | 66 | 24
4 | 82 | 30
6 | 84 | 31
8 | 82 | 31

After 8 minutes 98 % of bacteria were still infected.

(a) State the percentage of ³⁵S released after 4 minutes of blending. [1]
(b) Compare the release of ³⁵S and ³²P during blending. [2]
(c) Calculate the difference between the percentages of ³⁵S and ³²P remaining with the bacteria after 8 minutes. [2]
(d) Explain why the percentage of bacteria still infected is important in interpreting the results. [2]
(e) Explain what the results suggest about the nature of the genetic material. [3]
(f) Explain why radioactive sulfur and phosphorus were used as labels. [2]
items.answer: (a) 82 % (b) Both rise quickly in the first 2 minutes and then level off; far more ³⁵S (about 82 %) than ³²P (about 31 %) is released. (c) 51 percentage points (d) It shows that blending did not stop infection: the genetic material had already entered the cells, so the coats removed by blending (³⁵S) were not needed for infection. (e) DNA (³²P) mostly remains with/inside the bacteria while protein (³⁵S) is mostly removed; infection continues, so DNA is the material that enters and directs phage production. (f) Sulfur is found in proteins (some amino acids) but not DNA; phosphorus is in DNA (phosphate groups) but not in protein, so each label tracks one molecule.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 82 % (A1). (b) [2] Both increase then plateau (A1); ³⁵S release much greater than ³²P at each time (A1). (c) [2] ³²P remaining 69 %, ³⁵S remaining 18 % (M1); difference 51 (A1). (d) [2] Blending does not prevent infection (A1); so material in the supernatant (protein) is not required (R1). (e) [3] DNA enters cells (A1); protein stays outside (A1); DNA carries genetic information (R1). (f) [2] S in protein only (A1); P in DNA only (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about cell theory, microscopy and magnification calculations.

(a) Outline the meaning of the term "cryogenic electron microscopy". [1]

(b) Distinguish between electron microscopes and light microscopes. [2]

(c) Outline one way in which Robert Hooke’s observation of cork cells in 1665 shows the development of cell theory. [3]
items.answer: (a) Electron microscopy of samples frozen rapidly in vitreous ice, allowing the structure of proteins to be determined at near-atomic resolution (b) Light microscopes use light, have resolution about 200 nm, can view living cells in colour; electron microscopes use electron beams, resolve down to about 0.1–1 nm, need dead specimens in a vacuum and give black-and-white images. (c) Hooke saw small box-like compartments in cork and named them “cells”. His observations were among the first of many that led, by induction, to the generalisation that all organisms are made of cells.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] electron microscopy of samples frozen rapidly in vitreous ice, allowing the structure of proteins to be determined at near-atomic resolution. Award up to 1 mark for valid, linked points. (b) [2] Light microscopes use light, have resolution about 200 nm, can view living cells in colour; electron microscopes use electron beams, resolve down to about 0.1–1 nm, need dead specimens in a vacuum and give black-and-white images. Award up to 2 marks for valid, linked points. (c) [3] Context (Hooke saw small box-like compartments in cork and named them “cells”.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: His observations were among the first of many that led, by induction, to the generalisation that all organisms are made of cells. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the development of cell theory. Award up to 3 marks for valid, linked points.

items.stem:
This question is about karyotypes, genome size and whole-genome sequencing.

(a) Define the term "genome". [1]

(b) Distinguish between a genome and a karyotype. [2]

(c) "Organisms with more chromosomes are more complex." Explain the flaw in this statement. [3]
items.answer: (a) All the genetic information (DNA) of an organism or species (b) A karyotype describes the number and visible structure of chromosomes; a genome is the entire base sequence of the organism’s DNA. (c) Chromosome number does not reflect complexity: dogs have 78, humans 46 and some ferns over 1000.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] all the genetic information (DNA) of an organism or species. Award up to 1 mark for valid, linked points. (b) [2] A karyotype describes the number and visible structure of chromosomes; a genome is the entire base sequence of the organism’s DNA. Award up to 2 marks for valid, linked points. (c) [3] Chromosome number does not reflect complexity: dogs have 78, humans 46 and some ferns over 1000. Award up to 3 marks for valid, linked points.

items.stem:
This question is about organelles and compartmentalization; separation of nucleus and cytoplasm.

(a) Outline the meaning of the term "organelle". [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain how organelles can be separated by cell fractionation. [4]
items.answer: (a) A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function (b) Tissue is homogenised in cold, isotonic, buffered solution; filtered; centrifuged at increasing speeds; the densest/largest organelles (nuclei) form a pellet first, then mitochondria and chloroplasts, then lysosomes and ER, then ribosomes; each pellet can be studied. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: (a) [2] a discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function. Award up to 2 marks for valid, linked points. (b) [4] Award marks for: Tissue is homogenised in cold, isotonic, buffered solution; filtered; centrifuged at increasing speeds; the densest/largest organelles (nuclei) form a pellet first, then mitochondria and chloroplasts, then lysosomes and ER, then ribosomes; each pellet can be studied. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) Award up to 4 marks for valid, linked points.

items.stem:
This question is about habitats, adaptations and abiotic variables.

(a) Which is an example of a habitat? [2]

(b) Explain the difference between halophytes and xerophytes. [4]
items.answer: (a) a mangrove swamp on the coast of Kenya (b) Xerophytes are adapted to dry conditions (conserving water); halophytes are adapted to saline conditions (excluding or excreting salt).
items.markingKey: (a) [2] a mangrove swamp on the coast of Kenya. A place where organisms live. Award up to 2 marks for valid, linked points. (b) [4] Xerophytes are adapted to dry conditions (conserving water); halophytes are adapted to saline conditions (excluding or excreting salt). Award up to 4 marks for valid, linked points.

items.stem:
This question is about cohesion, adhesion and solvent properties of water.

(a) Explain why sodium chloride and glucose are transported dissolved in blood plasma whereas cholesterol and fats are not. [3]

(b) Zara writes: "Cohesion is the attraction between water and the walls of a container." Explain why this is inaccurate. [3]
items.answer: (a) NaCl is ionic and glucose is polar, so both are attracted to water and dissolve; cholesterol and fats are non-polar/hydrophobic, so they are carried in lipoprotein particles with a hydrophilic outer layer of phospholipids and proteins. (b) That is adhesion; cohesion is the attraction between water molecules themselves.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] Award marks for: NaCl is ionic and glucose is polar, so both are attracted to water and dissolve; cholesterol and fats are non-polar/hydrophobic, so they are carried in lipoprotein particles with a hydrophilic outer layer of phospholipids and proteins. Award up to 3 marks for valid, linked points. (b) [3] That is adhesion; cohesion is the attraction between water molecules themselves. Award up to 3 marks for valid, linked points.

items.stem:
This question is about classification hierarchy and the three domains.

(a) Which molecule did Carl Woese compare to propose the three-domain system? [2]

(b) Explain the difference between a natural classification and an artificial classification. [4]
items.answer: (a) ribosomal RNA (b) An artificial classification groups organisms by convenient features (e.g. habitat or flight) that may be due to convergence; a natural classification groups organisms by common ancestry so groups are clades.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] ribosomal RNA. Woese sequenced 16S rRNA in the 1970s. Award up to 2 marks for valid, linked points. (b) [4] An artificial classification groups organisms by convenient features (e.g. habitat or flight) that may be due to convergence; a natural classification groups organisms by common ancestry so groups are clades. Award up to 4 marks for valid, linked points.

items.stem:
This question is about ecological niches: obligate and facultative modes of nutrition.

(a) A student claims: "All bacteria need oxygen to survive." Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [4]

(b) Explain the difference between saprotrophic nutrition and holozoic nutrition. [5]

(c) "Classifying organisms by mode of nutrition is clear-cut." Discuss. [7]
items.answer: (a) Many bacteria are facultative or obligate anaerobes; some are killed by oxygen. (b) Holozoic organisms ingest food and digest it internally (e.g. animals); saprotrophs secrete enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the products externally (e.g. fungi). (c) The categories are useful but nutrition is a spectrum, and mixotrophs show the boundary is not clear-cut.
items.markingKey: (a) [4] Many bacteria are facultative or obligate anaerobes; some are killed by oxygen. Award up to 4 marks for valid, linked points. (b) [5] Holozoic organisms ingest food and digest it internally (e.g. animals); saprotrophs secrete enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the products externally (e.g. fungi). Award up to 5 marks for valid, linked points. (c) [7] Arguments for: most organisms clearly fit autotroph or heterotroph categories; the categories reflect fundamental differences in metabolism. Arguments against: mixotrophs such as Euglena and carnivorous plants use both modes; some parasitic plants have lost photosynthesis partly or completely. Supported judgement: The categories are useful but nutrition is a spectrum, and mixotrophs show the boundary is not clear-cut. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks. Award up to 7 marks for valid, linked points.

items.stem:
This question is about water as the medium for life: hydrogen bonding and polarity.

(a) Explain the difference between a polar covalent bond and a hydrogen bond. [4]

(b) Isabel writes: "Hydrogen bonds are the bonds that hold hydrogen and oxygen together inside a water molecule." Explain why this is inaccurate. [5]

(c) "Hydrogen bonding is the single most important reason why water is suitable as the medium for life." Discuss. [7]
items.answer: (a) A polar covalent bond is a strong intramolecular bond in which electrons are shared unequally (e.g. O–H within water); a hydrogen bond is a weak intermolecular attraction between δ+ H of one molecule and δ− O/N of another. (b) Inside a water molecule the bonds are polar covalent; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and δ− oxygen of another molecule. (c) Hydrogen bonding underlies most of water’s life-supporting properties, but polarity more generally, and planetary conditions that keep water liquid, are also required; it is the most important single molecular property rather than the only factor.
items.markingKey: (a) [4] A polar covalent bond is a strong intramolecular bond in which electrons are shared unequally (e.g. O–H within water); a hydrogen bond is a weak intermolecular attraction between δ+ H of one molecule and δ− O/N of another. Award up to 4 marks for valid, linked points. (b) [5] Inside a water molecule the bonds are polar covalent; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and δ− oxygen of another molecule. Award up to 5 marks for valid, linked points. (c) [7] Arguments for: cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat capacity, high latent heat and the density anomaly of ice all arise from hydrogen bonding; hydrogen bonds with solutes allow polar molecules such as sugars and amino acids to dissolve. Arguments against: the polarity of water (attraction to ions) explains the solubility of salts without hydrogen bonds; other factors such as the liquid range at Earth temperatures and the abundance of water on Earth are also essential. Supported judgement: Hydrogen bonding underlies most of water’s life-supporting properties, but polarity more generally, and planetary conditions that keep water liquid, are also required; it is the most important single molecular property rather than the only factor. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "organelle"?
options: The narrow space between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes where protons accumulate
A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function
A membrane-bound vesicle containing hydrolytic enzymes at low pH, used to digest materials
A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles
items.answer: A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function
items.markingKey: B. "organelle" is a discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function.

items.stem: Which statement about biodiversity at ecosystem, species and genetic levels is not correct?
options: Species richness is the number of different species present in an area.
Species richness is the number of species present.
A habitat with more species always has higher biodiversity according to Simpson’s index.
Species evenness is how similar the abundances of the different species in an area are.
items.answer: A habitat with more species always has higher biodiversity according to Simpson’s index.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “A habitat with more species always has higher biodiversity according to Simpson’s index.” – Simpson’s index also depends on evenness; a richer community dominated by one species can have a lower index than a less rich but even community.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "intermembrane space"?
options: Describes a stem cell able to differentiate into a limited range of related cell types (e.g. bone marrow stem cells)
The process by which unspecialised cells become specialised for a particular function by expressing particular genes
The narrow space between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes where protons accumulate
The specific microenvironment in the body that maintains stem cells and regulates their proliferation and differentiation
items.answer: The narrow space between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes where protons accumulate
items.markingKey: C. "intermembrane space" is the narrow space between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes where protons accumulate.

items.stem: Samples are mixed with anti-A and anti-B sera; agglutination shows which antigens are present. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (ABO blood typing before transfusion in hospitals)?
options: The roles of triglycerides
Lipids as energy stores
Cell recognition by glycoproteins
Glycogen as an energy store
items.answer: Cell recognition by glycoproteins
items.markingKey: C. Antibodies recognise specific carbohydrate antigens on red cells, so mismatched transfusion leads to agglutination and haemolysis.

items.stem: Which of these statements about simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis contains a misconception?
options: Isotonic is describes a solution with the same solute concentration (osmolarity) as the cell, so there is no net movement of water.
Osmosis is the net passive movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration.
Diffusion stops when the concentrations are equal because particles stop moving.
Aquaporin is a channel protein in the membrane that allows rapid passage of water molecules.
items.answer: Diffusion stops when the concentrations are equal because particles stop moving.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “Diffusion stops when the concentrations are equal because particles stop moving.” – Particles keep moving randomly; at equilibrium there is no net movement because movement is equal in both directions.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "deoxyribose"?
options: The early idea that DNA was a simple repeating sequence of the four bases in equal amounts, and so could not carry genetic information
The pyrimidine base found in RNA in place of thymine; it pairs with adenine
A nitrogenous base with a single-ring structure (cytosine, thymine or uracil)
The pentose sugar in DNA nucleotides, which lacks an oxygen (has H instead of OH) on carbon 2′
items.answer: The pentose sugar in DNA nucleotides, which lacks an oxygen (has H instead of OH) on carbon 2′
items.markingKey: D. "deoxyribose" is the pentose sugar in DNA nucleotides, which lacks an oxygen (has H instead of OH) on carbon 2′.

items.stem: Which of these statements about cell theory, microscopy and magnification calculations contains a misconception?
options: Magnification is how many times larger an image is than the actual object; magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
Electron microscopes can be used to watch living cells divide.
Resolution is the ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate; the minimum distance at which they can be seen as separate.
Detail depends on resolution.
items.answer: Electron microscopes can be used to watch living cells divide.
items.markingKey: B. The incorrect statement is “Electron microscopes can be used to watch living cells divide.” – Specimens for electron microscopy must be dead because they are fixed, stained and held in a vacuum.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "stomatal density"?
options: A part of a plant where sugars are produced or released, such as a photosynthesising leaf
The repeating contractile unit of a myofibril, between two Z lines
The number of stomata per unit area of leaf surface
The thin filament protein with binding sites for myosin heads
items.answer: The number of stomata per unit area of leaf surface
items.markingKey: C. "stomatal density" is the number of stomata per unit area of leaf surface.

items.stem: Archaea in the anaerobic rumen produce methane from CO₂ and hydrogen. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (methanogenic archaea in the rumen of cattle)?
options: Obligate anaerobic metabolism
Adaptations to a habitat
Fundamental and realised niches
Adaptations to saline, anaerobic soils
items.answer: Obligate anaerobic metabolism
items.markingKey: A. They can only live in oxygen-free environments and occupy a niche in the digestive system.

items.stem: Which of these statements about structure of DNA and RNA: nucleotides, bases and the double helix contains a misconception?
options: Double helix is the structure of DNA in which two antiparallel polynucleotide strands are wound around each other and held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
Nucleotide is the monomer of a nucleic acid, made of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.
Both strands of DNA run in the same direction.
Purines (adenine, guanine) have a double ring.
items.answer: Both strands of DNA run in the same direction.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “Both strands of DNA run in the same direction.” – The strands are antiparallel: one runs 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′.

items.stem: Which moon is a target in the search for extraterrestrial life because it has a liquid water ocean beneath its icy crust?
options: the Moon (Earth)
Io (Jupiter)
Phobos (Mars)
Europa (Jupiter)
items.answer: Europa (Jupiter)
items.markingKey: D. Europa and Enceladus are thought to have subsurface liquid water oceans.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about hershey-Chase and Chargaff's data: evidence for DNA as genetic material is false?
options: Chargaff’s rules is the observation that in double-stranded DNA the amount of adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine.
Most ³⁵S remained outside in the supernatant with the phage coats.
Tetranucleotide hypothesis is the early idea that DNA was a simple repeating sequence of the four bases in equal amounts, and so could not carry genetic information.
Chargaff’s rules apply to all nucleic acids.
items.answer: Chargaff’s rules apply to all nucleic acids.
items.markingKey: D. The incorrect statement is “Chargaff’s rules apply to all nucleic acids.” – The A = T and G = C ratios apply to double-stranded DNA; single-stranded DNA or RNA genomes need not follow them.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hydrogen bond"?
options: Describes non-polar substances that do not dissolve in water because they cannot form hydrogen bonds or ionic attractions with it
The attraction between molecules of different substances, such as water and the polar walls of xylem vessels
The ratio of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen in a sample of water, used to trace the source of Earth’s water
A weak intermolecular attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom of one polar molecule and a partially negative atom (such as oxygen or nitrogen) of another
items.answer: A weak intermolecular attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom of one polar molecule and a partially negative atom (such as oxygen or nitrogen) of another
items.markingKey: D. "hydrogen bond" is a weak intermolecular attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom of one polar molecule and a partially negative atom (such as oxygen or nitrogen) of another.

items.stem: From low to high tide line, kelp, mussels, limpets, barnacles and periwinkles occur in distinct bands. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (zonation on a rocky shore in Cape Town)?
options: Obligate anaerobic metabolism
The use of transects to study distribution
Mixotrophic nutrition
Adaptations to a habitat
items.answer: The use of transects to study distribution
items.markingKey: B. A transect up the shore reveals how tolerance of exposure and desiccation determines each species’ zone.

items.stem: Which statement about amino acids, peptide bonds and the diversity of polypeptides is not correct?
options: The R group is the variable part.
Peptide bonds are formed by hydrolysis.
Essential amino acid is an amino acid that cannot be synthesised by the body and must be obtained from the diet.
Peptide bond is the covalent bond formed by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of another.
items.answer: Peptide bonds are formed by hydrolysis.
items.markingKey: B. The incorrect statement is “Peptide bonds are formed by hydrolysis.” – Peptide bonds are formed by condensation (water released); hydrolysis breaks them.

items.stem: Which bonds stabilise α-helices and β-pleated sheets?
options: peptide bonds between R groups
disulfide bonds between cysteines
hydrogen bonds between groups of the polypeptide backbone
ionic bonds between phosphate groups
items.answer: hydrogen bonds between groups of the polypeptide backbone
items.markingKey: C. C=O and N–H of the backbone form hydrogen bonds.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about dichotomous keys and identification of species, including eDNA is false?
options: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is DNA shed by organisms into their surroundings (water, soil, air) that can be collected and sequenced to identify which species are present.
EDNA mainly shows presence/absence.
A dichotomous key can use as many choices as needed at each step.
DNA barcoding is identification of species using a short, standardised gene sequence (e.g. the COI mitochondrial gene in animals) compared with a reference database.
items.answer: A dichotomous key can use as many choices as needed at each step.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “A dichotomous key can use as many choices as needed at each step.” – A dichotomous key always offers exactly two contrasting choices at each step.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "in situ conservation"?
options: Conservation of species in their natural habitats, for example by establishing protected areas or nature reserves
A measure of species diversity, D = N(N − 1)/Σn(n − 1), that takes account of both richness and evenness
How similar the abundances of the different species in an area are
The variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations, including ecosystem, species and genetic diversity
items.answer: Conservation of species in their natural habitats, for example by establishing protected areas or nature reserves
items.markingKey: A. "in situ conservation" is conservation of species in their natural habitats, for example by establishing protected areas or nature reserves.

items.stem: A marsupial and a placental mammal evolved very similar skull shapes and body form as large predators. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (the thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus) and the grey wolf (Canis lupus))?
options: Sympatric speciation
Reproductive isolation and speciation
Convergent evolution
Homologous structures as evidence for evolution
items.answer: Convergent evolution
items.markingKey: C. Similar niches produced similar features despite the lineages having separated about 160 million years ago.

items.stem: Why does water have a high specific heat capacity?
options: Water is a non-polar molecule.
Energy is used to break hydrogen bonds before molecules can move faster.
Water molecules are very heavy.
Covalent bonds in water break as it heats.
items.answer: Energy is used to break hydrogen bonds before molecules can move faster.
items.markingKey: B. Absorbed energy first disrupts hydrogen bonds, so the temperature rises slowly.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "homeoviscous adaptation"?
options: Changes in membrane lipid composition, such as more unsaturated fatty acids in the cold, that maintain membrane fluidity
A membrane protein that uses energy (usually from ATP hydrolysis) to move specific particles against their concentration gradient
The net passive movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration
The movement of particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP and specific pump proteins
items.answer: Changes in membrane lipid composition, such as more unsaturated fatty acids in the cold, that maintain membrane fluidity
items.markingKey: A. "homeoviscous adaptation" is changes in membrane lipid composition, such as more unsaturated fatty acids in the cold, that maintain membrane fluidity.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about cladistics: clades, cladograms and molecular evidence is false?
options: Node is a branching point on a cladogram, representing a hypothetical common ancestor.
Present-day species are at the tips.
The more similar two species look, the more closely related they must be.
Shared derived characteristic is a feature that evolved in the common ancestor of a clade and is found in its descendants but not in more distant relatives.
items.answer: The more similar two species look, the more closely related they must be.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “The more similar two species look, the more closely related they must be.” – Similar appearance can result from convergent evolution; relationships are better shown by shared derived features and sequence data.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "autopolyploidy"?
options: Structures that have the same basic anatomy because they were inherited from a common ancestor, though they may have different functions
A limb with five digits and a common bone pattern (humerus, radius and ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) found in tetrapods
The condition of having more than two complete sets of chromosomes in a cell
Polyploidy in which the extra chromosome sets come from the same species, e.g. by failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis
items.answer: Polyploidy in which the extra chromosome sets come from the same species, e.g. by failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis
items.markingKey: D. "autopolyploidy" is polyploidy in which the extra chromosome sets come from the same species, e.g. by failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis.

items.stem: Glucose units are linked by condensation into branched glycogen molecules for storage. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (the synthesis of glycogen in liver cells after a meal)?
options: The structure–function relationship of cellulose
Lipids as energy stores
Glycogen as an energy store
Condensation reactions
items.answer: Condensation reactions
items.markingKey: D. Each new glycosidic bond formed releases a molecule of water, building a polymer from monomers.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about habitats, adaptations and abiotic variables is false?
options: Abiotic factors only affect plants.
A habitat is the place where an organism lives.
Adaptation is a heritable characteristic that increases an organism’s chance of survival and reproduction in its environment.
Halophyte is a plant adapted to grow in saline (salty) conditions, such as mangroves and salt-marsh plants.
items.answer: Abiotic factors only affect plants.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “Abiotic factors only affect plants.” – Abiotic factors such as temperature, water and oxygen availability affect all organisms, including animals and microbes.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Describes a stem cell able to differentiate into any cell type, including extra-embryonic tissues (e.g. the zygote)"?
options: cristae
thylakoid
type I pneumocyte
totipotent
items.answer: totipotent
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of totipotent.

items.stem: Which statement about evidence for evolution: base sequences, selective breeding and homologous structures is not correct?
options: Evolution is the cumulative change in the heritable characteristics of a population over time.
In natural selection the environment determines which variants survive and reproduce.
Vestigial structure is a reduced structure that had a function in an ancestor but has little or no function in the present organism.
Selective breeding creates new genes in the animals being bred.
items.answer: Selective breeding creates new genes in the animals being bred.
items.markingKey: D. The incorrect statement is “Selective breeding creates new genes in the animals being bred.” – Selective breeding selects among existing heritable variation (alleles); new alleles only arise by mutation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "natural classification"?
options: Identification of species using a short, standardised gene sequence (e.g. the COI mitochondrial gene in animals) compared with a reference database
A classification in which groups contain all the descendants of a common ancestor, reflecting evolutionary relationships
A domain of prokaryotes distinct from bacteria in rRNA sequence, membrane lipids and cell wall composition, many of which live in extreme environments
The science of naming, describing and classifying organisms
items.answer: A classification in which groups contain all the descendants of a common ancestor, reflecting evolutionary relationships
items.markingKey: B. "natural classification" is a classification in which groups contain all the descendants of a common ancestor, reflecting evolutionary relationships.

items.stem: Millions of hectares of forest were converted, reducing habitat for orang-utans, hornbills and many endemic species. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (deforestation of lowland rainforest in Borneo for oil palm plantations)?
options: Biodiversity at ecosystem, species and genetic levels
Habitat destruction as a cause of the biodiversity crisis
Ex situ conservation
Rewilding
items.answer: Habitat destruction as a cause of the biodiversity crisis
items.markingKey: B. Replacement of diverse forest by monoculture removes the niches species need, causing population declines and local extinctions.

items.stem: Which statement about cell size, surface area-to-volume ratio and adaptations of specialised cells is not correct?
options: Sperm are small, mobile, with a flagellum, mitochondria and acrosome.
Type I pneumocyte is an extremely thin alveolar cell adapted for gas exchange by diffusion.
Surface area-to-volume ratio is the surface area of a cell or organism divided by its volume; it decreases as size increases.
Larger cells have a larger SA:V ratio because they have more surface.
items.answer: Larger cells have a larger SA:V ratio because they have more surface.
items.markingKey: D. The incorrect statement is “Larger cells have a larger SA:V ratio because they have more surface.” – Larger cells have more surface area in absolute terms but a smaller SA:V ratio, because volume increases faster.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The movement of particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP and specific pump proteins"?
options: active transport
integral protein
phospholipid bilayer
pump protein
items.answer: active transport
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of active transport.

items.stem: Which statement about prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell structure; electron micrographs is not correct?
options: 70S ribosome is the smaller type of ribosome found in prokaryotes (and mitochondria and chloroplasts).
Plasmid is a small circle of DNA, separate from the main chromosome, found in many prokaryotes.
Prokaryotic cells have no ribosomes because they have no organelles.
Nucleoid is the region of a prokaryotic cell where the circular DNA is located, not enclosed by a membrane.
items.answer: Prokaryotic cells have no ribosomes because they have no organelles.
items.markingKey: C. The incorrect statement is “Prokaryotic cells have no ribosomes because they have no organelles.” – Prokaryotes do have ribosomes (70S); ribosomes are not membrane-bound, so they are present in all cells.

items.stem: Which two monosaccharides form sucrose?
options: fructose and galactose
glucose and galactose
two glucose molecules
glucose and fructose
items.answer: glucose and fructose
items.markingKey: D. Lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = two glucose.

items.stem: The hump stores up to 35 kg of fat, not water. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (the camel’s hump)?
options: Hydrolysis reactions
Condensation reactions
The structure–function relationship of cellulose
Lipids as energy stores
items.answer: Lipids as energy stores
items.markingKey: D. Fat is a compact energy store; its oxidation also produces metabolic water.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about complementary base pairing and the diversity of base sequences is false?
options: The genetic code is the sequence of bases in an individual’s DNA.
Genome is the whole of the genetic information of an organism.
Template strand is a strand of nucleic acid whose base sequence is used to build a complementary strand.
In DNA adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine.
items.answer: The genetic code is the sequence of bases in an individual’s DNA.
items.markingKey: A. The incorrect statement is “The genetic code is the sequence of bases in an individual’s DNA.” – The genetic code is the set of codon-to-amino-acid rules; the base sequence is the specific information that the code is used to read.

items.stem: Which gases were used in the Miller–Urey experiment to simulate the early atmosphere?
options: carbon dioxide and ozone
oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide
oxygen and water vapour only
methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour
items.answer: methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour
items.markingKey: D. A reducing atmosphere without free oxygen was assumed.

items.stem: Why does the I band shorten during contraction?
options: Actin filaments slide further over myosin, reducing the region containing actin only.
Myosin filaments shorten.
Actin filaments become shorter.
Z lines move apart.
items.answer: Actin filaments slide further over myosin, reducing the region containing actin only.
items.markingKey: A. Filaments slide, not shorten.

items.stem: Which property of water allows a continuous column of water to be pulled up xylem vessels?
options: the low viscosity of water
the high latent heat of vaporisation
cohesion between water molecules
the density anomaly of water
items.answer: cohesion between water molecules
items.markingKey: C. Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules together, so tension at the leaf pulls the column upwards.

items.stem: Mouse and human cells with differently labelled membrane proteins were fused; within 40 minutes the labels were intermixed. Which concept is best illustrated by this example (the Frye–Edidin cell fusion experiment (1970))?
options: The fluidity of membranes
Adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity
Facilitated diffusion of water
Endocytosis
items.answer: The fluidity of membranes
items.markingKey: A. Proteins diffuse laterally in the bilayer, supporting the fluid nature of the model.

items.stem: Why does the biological species concept not apply to bacteria?
options: Bacteria reproduce asexually, so interbreeding cannot be tested.
Bacteria have no DNA.
Bacteria are too small to be seen.
All bacteria are the same species.
items.answer: Bacteria reproduce asexually, so interbreeding cannot be tested.
items.markingKey: A. The concept relies on sexual reproduction.

items.stem:
On Daphne Major in the Galápagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the beak depth of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis). A severe drought in 1977 reduced the supply of small, soft seeds; mainly large, hard seeds remained.

Year | Population | Mean beak depth / mm
1976 | 1372 | 9.27
1977 | 223 | 9.83
1978 | — | 9.77

The standard deviation of beak depth in 1976 was 0.97 mm.

(a) Calculate the percentage of the 1976 population that survived to 1977. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in mean beak depth from 1976 to 1977. [2]
(c) Explain why the offspring produced in 1978 also had deeper beaks than the 1976 population. [2]
(d) The change in mean beak depth was about 0.6 standard deviations. Comment on the size of this change. [1]
(e) Suggest why this study is described as evolution being observed in action. [1]
(f) State the type of selection shown by these data. [1]
items.answer: (a) 16.3 % (b) +6.0 % (c) Beak depth is heritable; survivors passed alleles for deeper beaks to their offspring, so allele frequencies changed – evolution. (d) Large for one generation; shows strong directional selection. (e) The change in a heritable characteristic of the population was measured over a single generation, rather than inferred from fossils. (f) directional selection
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 223/1372 × 100 (M1) = 16.3 % (A1). (b) [2] (9.83 − 9.27)/9.27 × 100 (M1) = +6.0 % (A1). (c) [2] Heritability (A1); allele frequency change between generations (A1). (d) [1] Recognises a substantial shift relative to natural variation (A1). (e) [1] Measured directly across generations / short time scale (A1). (f) [1] Directional (A1).

items.stem:
Sofia measured six onion epidermal cells using an eyepiece graticule with the × 10 objective lens. A stage micrometer showed that at this magnification one eyepiece unit (epu) = 10.0 µm.

Cell | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Length / epu | 30 | 23 | 25 | 26 | 21 | 26

(a) Calculate the actual length of cell 1 in µm. [1]
(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the cell lengths. [1]
(c) The diameter of the field of view is 1800 µm. Estimate how many of the longest cells would fit across the field of view end to end. [1]
(d) Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be recalibrated when the objective lens is changed. [2]
(e) Suggest why a sample of at least six cells was measured. [2]
(f) Explain why a stage micrometer is needed to calibrate the eyepiece graticule. [2]
items.answer: (a) 300 µm (b) 30.6 µm (c) 6 (d) The graticule is in the eyepiece, so its divisions stay the same size while the specimen image is magnified by different amounts; the actual length represented by one epu changes. (e) Cells vary in size; a larger sample gives a more representative/reliable mean and allows variation (SD) to be estimated. (f) The stage micrometer has divisions of known size (10 µm), so the value of each eyepiece unit can be calculated at that magnification.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 30 × 10.0 = 300 µm (A1). (b) [1] SD (n − 1) = 30.6 µm (A1); accept population SD 27.9. (c) [1] 1800/300 = 6.0 → 6 whole cells (A1). (d) [2] Graticule scale fixed / specimen magnification changes (A1); epu value changes (A1). (e) [2] Biological variation (A1); reliable mean / representative (A1). (f) [2] Known scale (A1); calculation of eyepiece unit value (A1).

items.stem:
In experiments similar to Gause’s, Paramecium aurelia and P. caudatum were grown separately and then together in tubes of nutrient medium containing bacteria as food. The number of individuals per 0.5 cm³ was recorded.

Day | P. aurelia alone | P. caudatum alone | P. aurelia (mixed) | P. caudatum (mixed)
0 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2
2 | 11 | 8 | 10 | 7
4 | 51 | 29 | 47 | 26
6 | 140 | 73 | 129 | 40
8 | 200 | 114 | 184 | 46
10 | 216 | 132 | 199 | 33
12 | 219 | 137 | 201 | 14
14 | 220 | 139 | 202 | 0
16 | 220 | 139 | 202 | 0

(a) Calculate the mean rate of increase of P. aurelia alone between day 0 and day 8. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage difference between the final population of P. caudatum grown alone and in mixed culture. [2]
(c) Describe the growth of P. aurelia when grown alone. [2]
(d) State the principle illustrated by these results. [1]
(e) Suggest why P. aurelia in mixed culture reaches a slightly lower population than when grown alone. [1]
(f) Outline one limitation of applying these results to natural ecosystems. [1]
items.answer: (a) 24.8 individuals per 0.5 cm³ per day (b) -100 % (c) Slow initial increase, then rapid (exponential) growth, then levelling off at about 220 – sigmoid curve. (d) Competitive exclusion: two species with the same niche cannot coexist indefinitely. (e) Some food is consumed by P. caudatum before it is excluded. (f) Laboratory conditions are uniform and simple; in nature, habitat variation allows resource partitioning, and predators/disturbance may prevent exclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (200 − 2)/8 (M1) = 24.8 (A1). (b) [2] (0 − 139)/139 × 100 (M1) = -100 % (A1). (c) [2] Sigmoid shape (A1); plateau value from data (A1). (d) [1] Competitive exclusion (A1). (e) [1] Shared resource early on (A1). (f) [1] Valid limitation (A1).

items.stem:
Samples of a protease from the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis (enzyme X) and the same enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium (enzyme Y) were held at different temperatures for 10 minutes, cooled to 25 °C and their remaining activity measured as a percentage of the untreated activity.

Temperature / °C | Enzyme X activity remaining / % | Enzyme Y activity remaining / %
30 | 100 | 100
40 | 99 | 100
50 | 85 | 100
60 | 24 | 99
70 | 2 | 92
80 | 0 | 39
90 | 0 | 4

(a) State the activity of enzyme X remaining after treatment at 60 °C. [1]
(b) Compare the effect of temperature on enzymes X and Y. [2]
(c) Explain why activity was measured at 25 °C after cooling, rather than at the treatment temperature. [1]
(d) Explain the loss of activity of enzyme X at high temperatures. [3]
(e) Suggest how the structure of enzyme Y differs to make it more heat stable. [1]
items.answer: (a) 24 % (b) Both retain full activity at low temperatures and lose activity as temperature rises; Y tolerates much higher temperatures before losing activity. (c) It measures only the permanent (irreversible) loss of activity due to denaturation, not the temporary effect of temperature on reaction rate. (d) Heat breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds/hydrophobic interactions maintaining tertiary structure; active site changes shape; substrate no longer binds; denaturation. (e) More disulfide bonds, ionic bonds (salt bridges) and hydrophobic interactions; more compact core.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 24 % (A1). (b) [2] Similarity (A1); difference with data (A1). (c) [1] Separates denaturation from effect on rate (R1). (d) [3] Weak bonds broken (A1); shape/active site changed (A1); irreversible denaturation (A1). (e) [1] Any valid structural difference (A1).
